mcqs.question: Your team's RFCs attract plenty of thoughtful comments, but decisions keep drifting and work starts before anything is agreed. Which single change most reliably produces decisions?
options: Name one resolver in the header and announce the date the comment window closes
Add every engineer in the org as a reviewer so no perspective is missed
End each proposal with an open "thoughts?" so the discussion stays welcoming
Leave the document open indefinitely so a late objection is never lost
mcqs.explanation: An RFC only converges when someone is accountable for closing it and the debate has a deadline; those two fields are what turn an unbounded thread into a decision. Widening the reviewer list feels inclusive but does the opposite — a document addressed to everyone is reviewed by no one, and it adds comment volume without adding an endpoint.

mcqs.question: Your comment window closes tomorrow. SRE is listed as a required reviewer and has posted nothing. What is the correct read?
options: SRE has not reviewed it — chase them, because an unanswered required reviewer is a blocker, not a default approval
SRE has implicitly approved; no objection inside the window is consent
Drop SRE from the reviewer list so the announced deadline can still be met
Extend the window by three more weeks so every team has unlimited time
mcqs.explanation: Required reviewers are named precisely because their systems or on-call load change, so silence means unread, not agreed — the objection will arrive after launch instead. Treating silence as consent is the tempting shortcut and it is exactly how the team that gets paged at 3am ends up never having seen the proposal; extending the window indefinitely fails the other way, since a window that long stops functioning as a deadline at all.

mcqs.question: An RFC lists two staff engineers as approvers, and the two of them now disagree in the thread. Why is that arrangement itself the problem?
options: Approvers must always come from the same team as the author
Required reviewers are not permitted to leave comments on a proposal they approve
With two approvers nobody can unilaterally close the thread, so the outcome defaults to whoever argues longest
Staff engineers should give input on RFCs but never hold decision rights
mcqs.explanation: Decision rights have to be narrow enough that one person can end the discussion; splitting them between two peers removes the terminating condition and the process silently becomes decision-by-exhaustion. Seniority is not the issue — a staff engineer is usually the right resolver, there just has to be exactly one of them.

mcqs.question: Which of these "Alternatives considered" entries actually earns its place in an ADR?
options: "Redis was considered but was not the right fit for our needs at this time."
"We evaluated Redis, Memcached and Hazelcast in depth over a two-week spike."
"Redis is a mature, widely adopted choice with strong community support."
"Redis was rejected: the cache must survive a node restart, and our managed Redis tier offered no persistence option."
mcqs.explanation: A rejected alternative is only useful if a future reader can check whether the reason still holds — a named constraint like "must survive restart, tier had no persistence" can be re-evaluated when the tier changes. Describing how much effort went into the evaluation is the most tempting near-miss: it signals diligence but records no reason, so the next engineer learns nothing about why the option lost.

mcqs.question: RFC-0042 has just been accepted and the migration is starting. What should happen to the RFC document itself?
options: Freeze it read-only and write a one-page ADR that links back to it — the RFC is the debate, the ADR is the durable answer
Keep editing it as the system evolves so it always describes current reality
Delete it, since the shipped code is now the source of truth
Convert it into the team's runbook, because it already describes the new system
mcqs.explanation: The RFC is a snapshot of a debate at a moment in time and loses its meaning if you rewrite it later; the durable, greppable artifact is the short ADR that records the outcome and its costs. Keeping the RFC evergreen is the appealing wrong answer — it destroys the historical record of what was argued while producing documentation that drifts anyway.

mcqs.question: An ADR reads — Context: "we needed a scalable, modern event platform"; Decision: "we adopted Kafka"; Consequences: "improved scalability and reliability." What is its core defect?
options: It is far too short to count as a decision record
It names no specific force, no rejected alternative and no cost, so a reader learns nothing they could not infer from the code
It was written after the decision was made rather than before it
It uses ADR field names when a change of this size warranted an RFC header
mcqs.explanation: Every field is populated and none of them carries information: no incident or number in Context, no alternative with a checkable reason, and Consequences lists only upside. Being written after the fact is the tempting answer but is not the defect — ADRs are recorded after the decision by definition, and backfilling records for existing systems is legitimate; writing them from what you wish had happened is what breaks them.
